claims.source: Our recent photolabeling studies have confirmed that there are multiple PAM-NS-binding sites on α1β3 GABAARs (Chen et al., 2019). In addition to the canonical site at the interface between the TMDs of adjacent subunits (intersubunit site) (Chen et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2017; Laverty et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018), we identified NS-binding sites within the α-helical bundles of both the α1 and β3 subunits (intrasubunit sites) of α1β3 GABAARs (Chen et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior photolabeling studies by the authors.

claims.claim: 3α5αP binds to all three neurosteroid-binding sites (intersubunit and both intrasubunit sites) on α1β3 GABAARs.
claims.source: 3α5αP binds to all three sites (Chen et al., 2019); mutagenesis of these sites suggests that the intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites, but not the β3 intrasubunit site, contribute to 3α5αP PAM activity (Chen et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior photolabeling studies and mutational data in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites, but not the β3 intrasubunit site, contribute to 3α5αP PAM activity.
claims.source: 3α5αP binds to all three sites (Chen et al., 2019); mutagenesis of these sites suggests that the intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites, but not the β3 intrasubunit site, contribute to 3α5αP PAM activity (Chen et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior mutational studies and data in the manuscript (Figure 6B).

claims.claim: The 3α-hydroxyl group is critical to neurosteroid activation of GABAARs.
claims.source: The 3α-hydroxyl (3α-OH) group is critical to NS activation of GABAARs and 3β-OH NS lack PAM activity (Akk et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and data showing 3β5αP, KK148, and KK150 do not potentiate currents (Figure 1B-D).

claims.claim: 3β-OH neurosteroids lack PAM activity.
claims.source: The 3α-hydroxyl (3α-OH) group is critical to NS activation of GABAARs and 3β-OH NS lack PAM activity (Akk et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and data showing 3β5αP does not potentiate currents (Figure 1B).

claims.claim: Many 3β-OH neurosteroids are GABAAR NAMs.
claims.source: Indeed, many 3β-OH NS are GABAAR NAMs (Wang et al., 2002; Lundgren et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and data showing 3β5αP reduces steady-state currents (Figure 2C).

claims.claim: 3β-OH neurosteroids are non-competitive inhibitors with respect to GABA and 3α-OH neurosteroids.
claims.source: While molecular docking studies have suggested that the 3β-OH NS epi-pregnanolone (3β5βP) should compete for binding with PAM-NS (Miller et al., 2017), 3β-OH NS are non-competitive inhibitors with respect to GABA and 3α-OH NS, indicating that they are unlikely to act at the canonical PAM-binding site (Akk et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Steroids with a sulfate at the 3-carbon are GABAAR NAMs thought to act at sites distinct from GABAAR PAMs.
claims.source: Steroids with a sulfate rather than a hydroxyl at the 3-carbon are also GABAAR NAMs thought to act at sites distinct from GABAAR PAMs (Akk et al., 2007; Akk et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2002; Seljeset et al., 2018; Park-Chung et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Crystallographic studies have demonstrated a possible binding site for pregnenolone sulfate between TM3 and TM4 on the intracellular end of the α-subunit TMD.
claims.source: The precise location of this site is unclear, but crystallographic studies have demonstrated a possible binding site between TM3 and TM4 on the intracellular end of the α-subunit TMD (Seljeset et al., 2018; Laverty et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior crystallographic studies.

claims.claim: 3β-OH neurosteroids and pregnenolone sulfate likely act via interactions with distinct sites.
claims.source: While 3β-OH NS and PS both inhibit GABAARs, they likely act via interactions with distinct sites (Akk et al., 2007; Akk et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2002; Lundgren et al., 2003; Seljeset et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2017; Laverty et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: None of the neurosteroid analogues lacking a 3α-OH potentiated GABA-elicited currents.
claims.source: None of the NS analogues lacking a 3α-OH potentiated GABA-elicited currents (Figure 1B–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1B-D.

claims.claim: Both 3β5αP and KK148 significantly enhanced [3H]muscimol binding.
claims.source: However, both 3β5αP and KK148 significantly enhanced [3H]muscimol binding (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: Supported by radioligand binding data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: KK150 did not potentiate GABA-elicited currents and minimally enhanced [3H]muscimol binding.
claims.source: KK150, in contrast, did not potentiate GABA-elicited currents and minimally enhanced [3H]muscimol binding (Figure 1D–E).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological and radioligand binding data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claims.claim: Neurosteroid analogues with different stereochemistry or substituents at the 3- and 17-positions show distinct patterns in modulation of α1β3 GABAAR currents and orthosteric ligand binding.
claims.source: Collectively, these data show that, NS analogues with different stereochemistry or substituents at the 3- and 17-positions show distinct patterns in modulation of α1β3 GABAAR currents and orthosteric ligand binding.
claims.evidence: Supported by the combined electrophysiological and binding data for different neurosteroid analogues (Figure 1).

claims.claim: The 3-OH is an important determinant of binding affinity to the site(s) mediating neurosteroid enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding.
claims.source: Notably, the compounds with a 3-OH (3α5αP, 3β5αP) are 10-fold more potent than those with a 3-diazirine (KK148, KK150) in enhancing [3H]muscimol binding (Figure 1E), suggesting that the 3-OH is an important determinant of binding affinity to the site(s) mediating these effects.
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of EC50 values for different neurosteroids in [3H]muscimol binding assays (Figure 1E, Table 1).

claims.claim: KK148 enhanced [3H]muscimol binding in intact cells as much or more than in permeabilized cells.
claims.source: KK148 enhanced [3H]muscimol binding in intact cells as much or more than in permeabilized cells, indicating that this effect is not a result of selective NS actions on intracellular receptors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by radioligand binding data comparing intact and permeabilized cells shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: KK148 and 3β5αP both decreased steady-state currents when co-applied with saturating GABA.
claims.source: KK148 and 3β5αP both decreased steady-state currents (Figure 2A and C), whereas KK150 did not (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2A and 2C.

claims.claim: KK150 did not decrease steady-state currents when co-applied with saturating GABA.
claims.source: KK148 and 3β5αP both decreased steady-state currents (Figure 2A and C), whereas KK150 did not (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Co-application of 3β5αP with 1 mM GABA preferentially inhibited steady-state rather than peak currents.
claims.source: Co-application of 3β5αP with 1 mM GABA preferentially inhibited steady-state rather than peak currents (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The inhibitory effect of 3β5αP was not observed in receptors with the α1(V256S) TM2 pore-lining mutation.
claims.source: The inhibitory effect of 3β5αP was not observed in receptors with the α1(V256S) TM2 pore-lining mutation, which was previously shown to remove the inhibitory effects of sulfated steroids (Akk et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2002; Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2D and citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The α1(V256S)β3 mutation eliminated [3H]muscimol binding enhancement by 3β5αP but not 3α5αP.
claims.source: Consistent with this, the α1(V256S)β3 mutation which abolishes NS-induced inhibition (Akk et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2002) eliminated [3H]muscimol binding enhancement by 3β5αP but not 3α5αP (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by radioligand binding data shown in Figure 3 and citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: 3α5αP increases [3H]muscimol binding by stabilizing an active state of the receptor.
claims.source: We infer that 3α5αP increases [3H]muscimol binding by stabilizing an active state of the receptor.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that 3α5αP enhances binding and this effect is not eliminated by the α1(V256S) mutation that prevents desensitization.

claims.claim: 3β5αP increases [3H]muscimol binding by stabilizing a desensitized state of the receptor.
claims.source: In contrast, 3β5αP increases [3H]muscimol binding by stabilizing a desensitized state of the receptor; this effect is eliminated in the α1(V256S)β3 receptor.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that 3β5αP enhances binding and this effect is eliminated by the α1(V256S) mutation that prevents desensitization.

claims.claim: 3β5αP and KK148 enhance orthosteric ligand affinity by stabilizing a desensitized state of the GABAAR.
claims.source: These data indicate that 3β5αP and KK148 enhance orthosteric ligand affinity by stabilizing a desensitized state of the GABAAR.
claims.evidence: Supported by combined electrophysiological and binding data showing these compounds enhance [3H]muscimol binding and reduce steady-state currents.

claims.claim: Enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by 10 μM 3β5αP is slow, with a time constant of approximately 4 minutes at 4°C.
claims.source: Enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by 10 µM 3β5αP is slow, with a time constant of 4 min at 4°C (τ = 3.97 ± 0.15 min: mean ± SEM, n = 4, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by time course experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Application of 1 mM GABA elicited a current response with a peak Popen of 0.71 ± 0.25 in α1β3 GABAARs.
claims.source: Application of 1 mM GABA elicited a current response that had a peak Popen of 0.71 ± 0.25 (mean ± SD; n = 16).
claims.evidence: Calculated from electrophysiological recordings.

claims.claim: The steady-state Popen with 1 mM GABA was 0.121 ± 0.033 in α1β3 GABAARs.
claims.source: The Popen of the steady-state response was 0.121 ± 0.033 (n = 7), that was reduced to 0.077 ± 0.013 (n = 5) with 3 µM 3β5αP.
claims.evidence: Calculated from electrophysiological recordings.

claims.claim: 3 µM 3β5αP reduced steady-state Popen to 0.077 ± 0.013 in α1β3 GABAARs activated by 1 mM GABA.
claims.source: The Popen of the steady-state response was 0.121 ± 0.033 (n = 7), that was reduced to 0.077 ± 0.013 (n = 5) with 3 µM 3β5αP.
claims.evidence: Calculated from electrophysiological recordings.

claims.claim: The steady-state Pdesensitized is 0.829 in the presence of 1 mM GABA and 0.892 in the presence of GABA + 3β5αP.
claims.source: Analysis of steady-state currents using the Resting-Open-Desensitized model indicates that the steady-state Pdesensitized is 0.829 in the presence of GABA, and 0.892 in the presence of GABA + steroid.
claims.evidence: Calculated from electrophysiological data using a kinetic model.

claims.claim: Application of 20 nM muscimol elicited a peak response with Popen of 0.012 ± 0.004 in α1β3 GABAARs.
claims.source: The application of 20 nM muscimol elicited a peak response with Popen of 0.012 ± 0.004 (n = 6).
claims.evidence: Calculated from electrophysiological recordings.

claims.claim: 3 µM 3β5αP reduced the steady-state Popen from 0.011 ± 0.004 to 0.009 ± 0.004 in α1β3 GABAARs activated by 20 nM muscimol.
claims.source: The steady-state Popen was 0.011 ± 0.004. In the same cells, subsequent exposure to 3 µM 3β5αP reduced the steady-state Popen to 0.009 ± 0.004 (p=0.0174; paired t-test).
claims.evidence: Calculated from electrophysiological recordings.

claims.claim: The calculated steady-state Pdesensitized was 0.1001 in the presence of 20 nM muscimol and 0.2168 in the presence of muscimol + 3β5αP.
claims.source: The calculated steady-state Pdesensitized was 0.1001 in the presence of muscimol, and 0.2168 in the presence of muscimol + 3β5αP.
claims.evidence: Calculated from electrophysiological data using a kinetic model.

claims.claim: There is a predicted two-fold increase in the sum of (Popen + Pdesensitized) when 3β5αP is combined with 20 nM muscimol.
claims.source: Thus, there is a predicted two-fold increase in the sum of (Popen + Pdesensitized) when the steroid is combined with muscimol, consistent with the doubling of muscimol binding caused by 3β5αP in the [3H]muscimol binding experiments (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: Calculated from electrophysiological data and compared to binding data.

claims.claim: KK148, KK150, 3α5αP and 3β5αP all prevented KK200 photolabeling of α1N408 in the α1 intrasubunit site.
claims.source: KK148, KK150, 3α5αP and 3β5αP all prevented KK200 photolabeling of α1N408 in the α1 intrasubunit site (Figure 4B), consistent with their binding to this site.
claims.evidence: Supported by photolabeling competition experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: KK148, KK150 and 3α5αP but not 3β5αP prevented labeling of β3G308 in the intersubunit site.
claims.source: In contrast, KK148, KK150 and 3α5αP but not 3β5αP prevented labeling of β3G308 in the intersubunit site (Figure 4C), indicating that 3β5αP does not bind to the intersubunit site.
claims.evidence: Supported by photolabeling competition experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: KK148 and KK150 photolabeled Y415 in the α1 intrasubunit site.
claims.source: Product ion (MS2) spectra of the KK148- and KK150-labeled peptides from the α1 subunit identified the labeled residue as Y415 for both KK148 and KK150 with photolabeling efficiencies of 0.77% and 0.62%, respectively (Figure 4D–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2); Y415 is the same residue labeled by KK123 at the α1 intrasubunit site (Chen et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis of photolabeled peptides shown in Figure 4D-E.

claims.claim: KK148 and KK150 photolabeled the β3 intrasubunit site.
claims.source: The KK148 and KK150 labeled peptides in TM4 of the β3 subunit and corresponding unlabeled peptide were identified by fragmentation spectra as β3TM4 I426-N445. These data support labeling of the β3 intrasubunit site by KK148 and KK150.
claims.evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis of photolabeled peptides shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: 3β5αP completely inhibited KK123 photolabeling at both α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites.
claims.source: 3β5αP completely inhibited KK123 photolabeling at both intrasubunit sites (Figure 5B–C).
claims.evidence: Supported by photolabeling competition experiments shown in Figure 5B-C.

claims.claim: KK148, KK150 and 3α5αP bind to all three of the identified neurosteroid-binding sites.
claims.source: Collectively, the data show that KK148, KK150 and 3α5αP bind to all three of the identified NS-binding sites.
claims.evidence: Supported by photolabeling competition experiments (Figures 4 and 5).

claims.claim: 3β5αP selectively binds to the two intrasubunit binding sites, but not to the canonical β3(+)–α1(-) intersubunit site.
claims.source: In contrast, 3β5αP selectively binds to the two intrasubunit binding sites, but not to the canonical β3(+)–α1(-) intersubunit site.
claims.evidence: Supported by photolabeling competition experiments (Figures 4 and 5).

claims.claim: None of the mutations targeting neurosteroid-binding sites produced a significant change in [3H]muscimol Kd.
claims.source: None of these mutations produced a significant change in [3H]muscimol Kd (Figure 7B and Figure 7—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by radioligand binding isotherms shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Mutations in the β3(+)–α1(-) intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites decreased 3α5αP enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by approximately 80%.
claims.source: Mutations in the β3(+)–α1(-) intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites decreased 3α5αP enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by ~80%, while mutation of the β3 intrasubunit site led to a small decrease (Figure 6B, Table 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by radioligand binding data shown in Figure 6B and Table 1.

claims.claim: Mutation of the β3 intrasubunit site led to a small decrease in 3α5αP enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding.
claims.source: Mutations in the β3(+)–α1(-) intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites decreased 3α5αP enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by ~80%, while mutation of the β3 intrasubunit site led to a small decrease (Figure 6B, Table 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by radioligand binding data shown in Figure 6B and Table 1.

claims.claim: Mutations in the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites, but not the intersubunit site, decreased the enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by 3β5αP and KK148.
claims.source: In contrast, mutations in the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites, but not the intersubunit site decreased the enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by 3β5αP and KK148 (Figure 6C–D, Table 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by radioligand binding data shown in Figure 6C-D and Table 1.

claims.claim: The α1β3(M286W) mutation abolished [3H]muscimol binding enhancement by etomidate.
claims.source: The mutations targeting NS-binding sites resulted in modest decreases in [3H]muscimol binding enhancement by etomidate; however, the α1β3(M286W) mutation which abolishes etomidate potentiation and activation of GABAARs (Stewart et al., 2008; Ziemba et al., 2018), also abolished [3H]muscimol binding enhancement (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: Supported by radioligand binding data shown in Figure 6E and citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: KK150 inhibited enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by 3α5αP and KK148.
claims.source: Consistent with this prediction, KK150 inhibited enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by 3α5αP and KK148 (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: Supported by radioligand binding competition experiments shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Multiple neurosteroid-binding sites contribute to enhancement of [3H]muscimol affinity.
claims.source: Collectively, these results show that multiple NS-binding sites contribute to enhancement of [3H]muscimol affinity and that potentiating NS (3α5αP) and non-potentiating NS (3β5αP, KK148 and KK150) have both common and distinct sites of action.
claims.evidence: Supported by mutational analysis of different neurosteroid-binding sites (Figure 6, Table 1).

claims.claim: 3α5αP enhances [3H]muscimol binding through all three sites but predominantly through the intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites.
claims.source: Specifically, 3α5αP enhances [3H]muscimol binding through all three sites but predominantly through the intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites, which we have previously shown mediate PAM-NS potentiation (Chen et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by mutational analysis shown in Figure 6B and Table 1.

claims.claim: 3β5αP and KK148 enhance [3H]muscimol binding exclusively through the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites.
claims.source: In contrast, 3β5αP and KK148 enhance [3H]muscimol binding exclusively through the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites.
claims.evidence: Supported by mutational analysis shown in Figure 6C-D and Table 1.

claims.claim: KK150 antagonizes the effects of KK148 on [3H]muscimol binding, presumably via the intrasubunit sites.
claims.source: KK150 antagonizes the effects of KK148 on [3H]muscimol binding, presumably via the intrasubunit sites, and antagonizes the effects of 3α5αP, possibly via all three sites.
claims.evidence: Supported by competition binding experiments shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: KK150 antagonizes the effects of 3α5αP on [3H]muscimol binding, possibly via all three sites.
claims.source: KK150 antagonizes the effects of KK148 on [3H]muscimol binding, presumably via the intrasubunit sites, and antagonizes the effects of 3α5αP, possibly via all three sites.
claims.evidence: Supported by competition binding experiments shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Membranes containing WT receptors have 10–20-fold higher [3H]muscimol binding (Bmax) than membranes containing α1(N408A/Y411F)β3 receptors.
claims.source: The raw data show that membranes containing WT receptors have 10–20-fold higher [3H]muscimol binding (Bmax) than membranes containing α1(N408A/Y411F)β3 receptors (Figure 7A), whereas the Bmax of membranes containing α1(Q242L)β3, α1β3(Y284F) or α1(V227W)β3 receptors was the same as for WT α1β3 GABAARs (Figure 7—source data 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by radioligand binding isotherms shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: The α1(N408A/Y411F)β3 mutations did not have a significant effect on [3H]muscimol affinity.
claims.source: The α1(N408A/Y411F)β3 mutations did not have a significant effect on [3H]muscimol affinity (Figure 7B), but eliminated the modulatory effects of NS (3α5αP and KK148) on [3H]muscimol affinity (Figure 7C–D and Figure 7—source data 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by normalized radioligand binding isotherms shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: The α1(N408A/Y411F)β3 mutations eliminated the modulatory effects of neurosteroids (3α5αP and KK148) on [3H]muscimol affinity.
claims.source: The α1(N408A/Y411F)β3 mutations did not have a significant effect on [3H]muscimol affinity (Figure 7B), but eliminated the modulatory effects of NS (3α5αP and KK148) on [3H]muscimol affinity (Figure 7C–D and Figure 7—source data 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by radioligand binding isotherms with and without neurosteroids shown in Figure 7C-D.

claims.claim: Etomidate enhanced [3H]muscimol affinity in both the WT and α1(N408A/Y411F)β3 receptors.
claims.source: Etomidate enhanced [3H]muscimol affinity in both the WT and α1(N408A/Y411F)β3 receptors, indicating that the effect of these mutations are specific to NS action (Figure 7C–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by radioligand binding isotherms with etomidate shown in Figure 7C-D.

claims.claim: 3β5αP produced a small reduction in steady-state current in α1(Q242L)β3 receptors.
claims.source: 3α5αP produced a small reduction in steady-state current in α1(Q242L)β3 receptors with mutations in neither of the intrasubunit sites (Figure 10A).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 10A.

claims.claim: The inhibitory effect of 3α5αP in α1(Q242L)β3 receptors was eliminated by α1(V256S)β3.
claims.source: This inhibitory effect was eliminated by α1(V256S)β3, indicating that it was due to receptor desensitization (Figure 10D).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 10D.

claims.claim: In receptors with combined mutations in the intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites, 3α5αP significantly inhibited the steady-state current.
claims.source: In receptors with combined mutations in the intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites [i.e. α1(Q242L/N408A/Y411F)β3], 3α5αP significantly inhibited the steady-state current (Figure 10B), an effect that was markedly reduced by mutations in the β3 intrasubunit site [α1(Q242L)β3(Y284F)] (Figure 10C).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 10B.

claims.claim: The inhibitory effect of 3α5αP in α1(Q242L/N408A/Y411F)β3 receptors was markedly reduced by mutations in the β3 intrasubunit site.
claims.source: In receptors with combined mutations in the intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites [i.e. α1(Q242L/N408A/Y411F)β3], 3α5αP significantly inhibited the steady-state current (Figure 10B), an effect that was markedly reduced by mutations in the β3 intrasubunit site [α1(Q242L)β3(Y284F)] (Figure 10C).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 10C.

claims.claim: 3α5αP exerts a desensitizing effect by binding to the β3 intrasubunit site.
claims.source: These data suggest that 3α5αP exerts a desensitizing effect by binding to the β3 intrasubunit site and that 3α5αP binding to the α1 intrasubunit site does not promote desensitization (Figure 10D).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings with various mutations shown in Figure 10.

claims.claim: 3α5αP binding to the α1 intrasubunit site does not promote desensitization.
claims.source: These data suggest that 3α5αP exerts a desensitizing effect by binding to the β3 intrasubunit site and that 3α5αP binding to the α1 intrasubunit site does not promote desensitization (Figure 10D).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings with various mutations shown in Figure 10.

claims.claim: Enhanced desensitization by the PAM-NS 3α5αP has been observed in prior studies.
claims.source: Enhanced desensitization by the PAM-NS 3α5αP (Haage and Johansson, 1999) and 3α5α-THDOC (Zhu and Vicini, 1997; Bianchi and Macdonald, 2003) has been observed in prior studies supporting the current finding with 3α5αP.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The selective binding of 3β5αP to a subset of identified neurosteroid-binding sites provides an explanation for its NAM activity.
claims.source: The selective binding of 3β5αP to a subset of identified NS-binding sites provides an explanation for its NAM activity.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the combined photolabeling and functional data showing 3β5αP binds only to intrasubunit sites and promotes desensitization.

claims.claim: 3β5αP stabilizes desensitized receptors by binding to the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites.
claims.source: 3β5αP stabilizes desensitized receptors by binding to the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites, but does not activate the receptor because it does not bind to the intersubunit site.
claims.evidence: Supported by photolabeling data showing 3β5αP binds to intrasubunit sites (Figures 4-5) and functional data showing it promotes desensitization (Figure 9).

claims.claim: 3β5αP does not activate the receptor because it does not bind to the intersubunit site.
claims.source: 3β5αP stabilizes desensitized receptors by binding to the α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites, but does not activate the receptor because it does not bind to the intersubunit site.
claims.evidence: Supported by photolabeling data showing 3β5αP does not bind to the intersubunit site (Figure 4C) and functional data showing it does not potentiate currents (Figure 1B).

claims.claim: Docking and free energy perturbation calculations predicted that 3β5βP binds to the intersubunit site with free energies equivalent to pregnanolone.
claims.source: First, docking and free energy perturbation calculations in a prior study predicted that 3β5βP binds to the intersubunit site in a similar orientation and with free energies of binding that are equivalent to pregnanolone (3α5βP) (Miller et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior computational study.

claims.claim: Docking studies show similar binding energies and orientations of 3β5αP and 3α5αP binding in the β3(+)–α1(-) intersubunit site.
claims.source: Our docking studies also show similar binding energies and orientations of 3β5αP and 3α5αP binding in the β3(+)–α1(-) intersubunit site of either a homology model of the α1β3 receptor or the cryo-EM structure (PDB ID: 6I53) of the α1β3γ2 receptor in a lipid nanodisc (Laverty et al., 2019; Figure 11).
claims.evidence: Supported by computational docking studies shown in Figure 11.

claims.claim: Binding affinity or docking scores of neurosteroids binding to the intersubunit site are not significantly affected by mutations that eliminate neurosteroid activation.
claims.source: We have also shown that binding affinity or docking scores of NS binding to the intersubunit site are not significantly affected by mutations (α1Q242L, α1Q242W, α1W246L) that eliminate NS activation, although binding orientation is altered (Sugasawa et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior study by the authors.

results.result: Allopregnanolone (3α5αP) binds to the canonical β3(+)–α1(-) intersubunit site in α1β3 GABAA receptors, whereas epi-allopregnanolone (3β5αP) does not bind to this site.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, and C66 are directly supported by photolabeling competition experiments (Figure 4C) showing that 3α5αP prevents KK200 photolabeling of β3G308 in the intersubunit site while 3β5αP does not. This differential binding provides a mechanistic explanation for the distinct functional properties of these epimeric neurosteroids.

results.result: Both allopregnanolone and epi-allopregnanolone bind to intrasubunit sites in both the α1 and β3 subunits, with 3β5αP selectively binding only to these intrasubunit sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C65, C69, and C71 are supported by photolabeling competition experiments showing that both steroids prevent KK123 and KK200 photolabeling at α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites (Figures 4B, 5B-C). The selective binding of 3β5αP to only intrasubunit sites (not intersubunit) is well-documented across multiple experiments.

results.result: Binding of neurosteroids to α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites promotes receptor desensitization, with mutations in these sites preventing approximately 67% of 3β5αP-enhanced desensitization.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C55, C94, C95, C126-C129 are supported by electrophysiological data (Figure 9B) showing that mutations in α1 and β3 intrasubunit sites reduce 3β5αP-enhanced desensitization by ~67%, while intersubunit site mutations have no effect. The combined mutational and functional data provide strong evidence for the role of intrasubunit sites in desensitization.

results.result: KK148 and KK150 bind to all three neurosteroid-binding sites on α1β3 GABAARs but do not potentiate GABAAR currents.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C67, C68, and C70 are supported by photolabeling competition experiments (Figure 4B-C) and direct photolabeling showing adducts at α1Y415 and β3 intrasubunit sites (Figure 4D-E), combined with electrophysiological recordings (Figure 1C-D) showing no potentiation. The data demonstrate that binding to the intersubunit site is insufficient for activation.

results.result: KK148 is a desensitizing agent that enhances [3H]muscimol binding and reduces steady-state currents.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C43, C48, and C133 are supported by electrophysiological data showing KK148 reduces steady-state currents (Figure 2A) with 27.2 ± 6.0% desensitization, and radioligand binding data showing significant enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding (Figure 1E). The functional and binding data are consistent with KK148 stabilizing a desensitized state.

results.result: KK150 is devoid of allosteric activity, showing minimal enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding and no effect on steady-state currents.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C44, C49, and C135 are supported by electrophysiological data showing KK150 does not reduce steady-state currents (Figure 2B) with only 2.1 ± 0.7% desensitization, and minimal enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding (Figure 1E). This suggests KK150 binds to all three sites without efficacy, making it a potential neurosteroid antagonist scaffold.

results.result: Differential occupancy and efficacy at three discrete neurosteroid-binding sites determine whether a neurosteroid has potentiating, inhibitory, or competitive antagonist activity on GABAARs.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C121, and C122 represent the central conclusion of the manuscript, supported by the combined photolabeling, binding, and electrophysiological data showing different neurosteroids bind to different subsets of sites with different functional outcomes. The site-selectivity and state-dependence model is well-supported by the experimental evidence.

results.result: Mutations in neurosteroid-binding sites differentially affect enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by 3α5αP versus 3β5αP/KK148, with 3α5αP acting predominantly through intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit sites, while 3β5αP and KK148 act exclusively through intrasubunit sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75, C78-C80 are supported by mutational analysis showing that intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit site mutations decrease 3α5αP enhancement by ~80% (Figure 6B, Table 1), while α1 and β3 intrasubunit site mutations decrease 3β5αP and KK148 enhancement (Figure 6C-D). The differential effects provide strong evidence for site-specific mechanisms.

results.result: KK150 antagonizes enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by 3α5αP and KK148, acting as a competitive neurosteroid antagonist at all three binding sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C77, C81, C82, and C104 are supported by radioligand binding competition experiments (Figure 8) showing KK150 inhibits enhancement by both 3α5αP and KK148. The antagonism is consistent with the model that KK150 binds to all three sites without efficacy, though the precise mechanism at each site requires further investigation.

results.result: 3α5αP exerts a desensitizing effect by binding to the β3 intrasubunit site, while binding to the α1 intrasubunit site does not promote desensitization.
results.evaluation: Claims C91, C92, and C87-C90 are supported by electrophysiological recordings with various mutations (Figure 10) showing that 3α5αP inhibits steady-state current in receptors with combined intersubunit and α1 intrasubunit site mutations, and this effect is reduced by β3 intrasubunit site mutations. The data demonstrate site-specific functional effects of 3α5αP binding.

results.result: The α1(V256S)β3 mutation differentially affects [3H]muscimol binding enhancement by 3β5αP versus 3α5αP, with 3α5αP stabilizing an active state and 3β5αP stabilizing a desensitized state.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 are supported by radioligand binding data (Figure 3) showing that the α1(V256S) mutation eliminates 3β5αP enhancement but not 3α5αP enhancement. The differential effects provide evidence that these epimeric neurosteroids stabilize different receptor conformational states, though the inference about specific states is based on indirect evidence.

results.result: Neurosteroid analogues lacking a 3α-OH do not potentiate GABA-elicited currents, but show distinct patterns in modulation of orthosteric ligand binding, with the 3-OH being an important determinant of binding affinity.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C46 are supported by electrophysiological recordings (Figure 1B-D) showing no potentiation by 3β5αP, KK148, or KK150, and radioligand binding data (Figure 1E, Table 1) showing that 3-OH compounds are 10-fold more potent than 3-diazirine compounds. The data demonstrate the importance of the 3α-OH for activation while showing that binding can occur without it.

results.result: KK148 and 3β5αP decrease steady-state currents when co-applied with saturating GABA, with 3β5αP preferentially inhibiting steady-state rather than peak currents, and this effect is eliminated by the α1(V256S) mutation.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 are supported by electrophysiological recordings (Figure 2A, 2C, 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) showing that KK148 and 3β5αP reduce steady-state currents, with 3β5αP preferentially affecting steady-state over peak currents. The elimination of the effect by α1(V256S) mutation supports the interpretation that these compounds promote desensitization rather than channel block.

results.result: Quantitative analysis of electrophysiological data using the Resting-Open-Desensitized model shows that 3β5αP increases the probability of desensitized receptors, with predicted changes consistent with observed enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C64 are supported by electrophysiological recordings and kinetic modeling showing that 3β5αP increases Pdesensitized from 0.829 to 0.892 at high GABA and from 0.1001 to 0.2168 at low muscimol concentrations. The predicted two-fold increase in (Popen + Pdesensitized) at low agonist is consistent with the doubling of muscimol binding (Figure 1E), providing quantitative support for the desensitization mechanism.

results.result: Enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding by 10 μM 3β5αP is slow, with a time constant of approximately 4 minutes at 4°C.
results.evaluation: Claim C56 is supported by time course experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) showing τ = 3.97 ± 0.15 min. The slow time course is interpreted as being rate-limited by the transition from resting to active to desensitized states rather than by 3β5αP binding itself, though this interpretation is speculative.

results.result: The α1(N408A/Y411F)β3 mutations do not affect [3H]muscimol affinity but eliminate neurosteroid modulation while preserving etomidate effects, indicating specificity for neurosteroid action at the α1 intrasubunit site.
results.evaluation: Claims C72, C83-C86 are supported by radioligand binding isotherms (Figure 7) showing that α1(N408A/Y411F)β3 mutations eliminate neurosteroid enhancement of [3H]muscimol binding without affecting basal affinity or etomidate effects. The preservation of etomidate effects demonstrates that the mutations specifically disrupt neurosteroid action rather than causing general receptor dysfunction.

results.result: KK148 enhances [3H]muscimol binding in intact cells as much or more than in permeabilized cells, indicating that this effect is not due to selective actions on intracellular receptors.
results.evaluation: Claim C47 is supported by radioligand binding data comparing intact and permeabilized cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). This control experiment addresses the potential confound that the binding assays measure total receptors while electrophysiology measures only surface receptors, ruling out selective intracellular effects.

results.result: The α1β3(M286W) mutation abolishes [3H]muscimol binding enhancement by etomidate, serving as a positive control for site-specific effects.
results.evaluation: Claim C76 is supported by radioligand binding data (Figure 6E) and citations to prior literature showing that this mutation abolishes etomidate effects. This serves as an important positive control demonstrating that the assay can detect loss of allosteric modulator effects when the appropriate binding site is disrupted.

results.result: Computational docking studies show similar binding energies and orientations of 3β5αP and 3α5αP in the β3(+)–α1(-) intersubunit site, with a rank order affinity of intersubunit > α1 intrasubunit > β3 intrasubunit sites for 3α5αP.
results.evaluation: Claims C98 and C111 are based on computational docking studies (Figure 11, Figure 11—source data 1). While the docking shows similar binding energies for 3β5αP and 3α5αP at the intersubunit site, this contradicts the experimental photolabeling data showing 3β5αP does not bind to this site. The discrepancy between computational predictions and experimental results indicates limitations in the docking approach and suggests the binding selectivity may be due to factors not captured in the models (e.g., membrane lipid effects, conformational state-dependence).

results.result: The desensitizing effect of 3β5αP is completely eliminated by the α1(V256S)β3 mutation but not completely eliminated by combined mutations of all three binding sites, suggesting either incomplete mutation effects or additional unidentified binding sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C132 are supported by electrophysiological data (Figure 9B) showing differential effects of mutations. However, the interpretation is uncertain because the incomplete elimination by combined site mutations could reflect either incomplete disruption of binding by the mutations or the existence of additional sites. Further experiments would be needed to distinguish between these possibilities.

results.result: Background claims about neurosteroids as endogenous modulators, their clinical uses, and their principal target being GABAARs.

results.result: Background claims about GABAAR structure, prior evidence for neurosteroid binding sites, and previous findings from the authors' work.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C34 are background claims about GABAAR structure and prior evidence for neurosteroid binding sites, supported by citations to prior literature including the authors' previous work. These establish the foundation for the current study and are appropriately documented.

results.result: Background claims about the importance of the 3α-hydroxyl group and prior evidence for distinct binding sites for different neurosteroid classes.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C41 are background claims about the structural requirements for neurosteroid activity and prior evidence for distinct binding sites, supported by citations to prior literature. These provide important context for interpreting the current findings regarding site-selective binding.

results.result: Background claims about prior observations of neurosteroid effects on desensitization and synaptic function, and analogous findings in bacterial pLGICs.
results.evaluation: Claims C93, C101, and C105-C110 are background claims about prior observations of neurosteroid effects on desensitization and synaptic function, supported by citations to prior literature. These provide context for the functional significance of the current findings and draw parallels to related systems.

results.result: Background claims about prior computational and structural studies of neurosteroid binding, including limitations of available structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C97, C99, C100, C114-C116 are background claims about prior computational and structural studies, supported by citations to prior literature. These provide context for the limitations of current structural understanding and the need for the photolabeling approach used in this study.

results.result: The effects of various neurosteroid analogues are a consequence of their efficacy at each site they occupy, with KK148 predicted to act as a competitive antagonist to PAM-NS at the intersubunit site.
results.evaluation: Claims C102 and C103 represent inferences from the combined data. C102 is well-supported by the mutational, binding, and functional data. C103 is a prediction from the model that KK148 binds to the intersubunit site without efficacy, which is reasonable but not directly tested in the manuscript.

results.result: Mutational analysis indicates that 3α5αP has lower affinity for the β3 intrasubunit site, which may serve as a negative feedback mechanism preventing excessive PAM-NS effects.
results.evaluation: Claim C112 is supported by mutational analysis (Figure 6B, Table 1) showing smaller effects of β3 intrasubunit site mutations. Claim C113 is speculative but reasonable based on the observation that 3α5αP binding to this site promotes desensitization. The negative feedback hypothesis is plausible but would require additional experiments to test directly.

results.result: Discussion of potential differences in neurosteroid binding and effects in trimeric (αβγ) versus dimeric (αβ) GABAARs, including the influence of the γ-subunit on receptor symmetry.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C120 are speculative discussions about potential differences in trimeric receptors, based on established knowledge and inference from the current study. While the speculation is reasonable, the manuscript does not provide direct experimental evidence for these claims. The discussion appropriately acknowledges these as limitations and areas for future investigation.

results.result: Speculation about future directions, including the likelihood of additional neurosteroid-binding sites in other GABAAR subtypes and the potential for developing precision neurosteroid therapeutics.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C125 are speculative statements about future directions and potential applications. While these are reasonable extrapolations from the current findings, they are not directly supported by data in the manuscript. These represent appropriate forward-looking statements in the discussion but should not be evaluated as supported results.
